title: Norway Seeks Temporary Ban on Smart Glasses
paragraphs: Smart glasses that can take photos, record videos and use artificial intelligence are becoming increasingly popular. However, Norway is now planning to temporarily ban them in certain public places because of concerns about privacy.

On October 5, 2026, the Norwegian government announced that it would ask the country's parliament to approve a temporary ban on AI glasses in selected places. According to reports, these could include hospitals and other healthcare facilities, gyms with changing rooms and showers, schools, kindergartens, playgrounds and youth clubs. Places such as parks, beaches, museums, shopping centers, concerts and sporting events are also being considered.

However, the government stressed that it is not proposing a total ban. People would still be allowed to use smart glasses in some places and for private purposes. The government is also considering exceptions for vulnerable groups, so that smart glasses could still be used in ways that benefit society. In addition, a temporary ban would give the authorities time to decide which devices should be covered and whether permanent rules are needed. The government has also appointed a group of experts to advise on permanent rules for wearable technology.

The main concern is that smart glasses look very similar to ordinary glasses, so people do not always know when they are being recorded. Meta, which sells smart glasses made with Ray-Ban, uses a small light that shows when the glasses are recording, and it disables the camera if the light is covered. However, concerns remain. For example, Instagram has removed videos and accounts linked to people who used the glasses to harass strangers. Before the national government's announcement, the city of Oslo had already banned smart glasses in schools for the entire school day, starting on August 27, 2026. Julie Remen Midtgarden, Oslo's deputy mayor for education, said the city refused to allow its children to become extras in Meta's data collection. Midtgarden also criticized the national government for studying the issue instead of acting, pointing out that the glasses were already being used in Norwegian schoolyards.

If the law is approved, Norway could become one of the first countries in the world to restrict AI glasses in public places. However, the bill had not yet been voted on by parliament at the time of the announcement.
